title: Repeated Exposure to COVID-19 Misinformation: A Longitudinal Analysis of Prevalence and Predictors in a Community Sample
screen_reason: Weekly panel survey (iHeard St. Louis, n = 213 adults, August 2021 to August 2022) asking whether respondents had heard, read or seen each of five inaccurate COVID-19 vaccine claims in the past week. Table 1 gives, for each claim, the number and share of panelists who reported hearing it at least once across the weeks it was assessed. These are self-reported exposure shares with clear denominators: RECALL (exposure).

estimates.country: St. Louis City and County, Missouri, USA
estimates.measure_type: % of panelists who reported hearing the 'natural immunity' COVID-19 vaccine claim at least once over 23 weekly surveys
estimates.value_raw: 139/173 (80.35%) heard it 1 time or more; 34 (19.65%) never heard it
estimates.denominator: 173 panelists who ever answered this item (convenience community panel of adults living or working in St. Louis City or County, MO)
estimates.definition: Answered 'Yes' in at least one week to 'In the last week, have you heard, read or seen something like this: People who have had COVID don't need to get vaccinated because they already have natural immunity?'
estimates.misinfo_def: "5 COVID-19 misinformation items" described as "inaccurate claims" about natural immunity, duration of vaccine protection, booster shots, Omicron and vaccinating children
estimates.source_quote: Natural immunity—People who have had COVID don’t need to get vaccinated because they already have “natural immunity”. (n = 173) 23 (2021-10-03, 2022-03-06) 34 (19.65%) 139 (80.35%)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported weekly exposure; items were pre-selected inaccurate claims circulating locally, identified by the iHeard misinformation surveillance system. Average weekly response rate 90%.
estimates.moderator_quote: Each week from August 2021 to August 2022, panel members (n = 213, age ≥ 18; living or working in St. Louis City or County, MO) were asked, “In the last week, have you heard, read 66 or seen something like this: <misinformation item>?”
estimates.notes: Denominator is the number who ever answered this item (173), not the full panel of 213. The body text rounds this to 'Eighty percent'. The OCR of the survey stem contains a stray '66'.

missed_or_uncertain: The paper's headline is repeated exposure: the share hearing each claim in 3 or more different weeks (natural immunity 75/173 = 43.35%; vaccine doesn't last 51/163 = 31.29%; vaccine doesn't work 27/134 = 20.15%; Omicron 40/150 = 26.67%; kids at low risk 20/197 = 10.15%), summarised in the abstract as '10%-43% of respondents reported hearing the misinformation in >= 3 different weeks'. These are stricter definition variants of the five rows extracted here; they were left out to keep one exposure estimate per claim, but could defensibly be added as definition_variant rows. The 2-times-or-more, 4, 5 and 6-times-or-more columns of Table 1 are further variants of the same. Also not extracted: the mean number of sources per claim (2.1-2.5), which is a count not a share; and all incidence rate ratios for frontline workers, age, and race, which are associations rather than prevalence shares.

rob.design: Convenience panel (iHeard St. Louis) of 213 adults recruited through local partner organisations, oversampling African American residents (38% vs 29% of the local population); weekly mobile phone surveys August 2021 to August 2022; average weekly response rate 90%; five misinformation items each asked for 10 to 23 consecutive weeks; item-level denominators vary (134-197) because not everyone answered every item. Exposure is self-reported, single item per claim, no validation of reported exposure. Negative binomial models with an offset for the number of weeks answered. Authors flag convenience sampling as limiting generalizability.
rob.item6_quote: We selected for analysis 5 COVID-19 misinformation items that were asked for ≥ 10 consecutive weeks (max = 23 weeks).
rob.item10_quote: Eighty percent of panel members had heard the “nat- ural immunity” claim at least once in the 23 weeks it was assessed; only 30% had heard the “kids at low risk” claim during the 10 weeks it was assessed (Table 1).
